claims.text: The alloy begins as a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
Sustained high mechanical loading induces localized compositional segregation in the alloy.
Localized compositional segregation nucleates brittle nanoscale precipitates at stress-concentration sites.
The nanoscale precipitates act as crack-initiation points.
Crack initiation at the precipitates reduces toughness and promotes brittle fracture.
High mechanical stresses promote local atomic mobility and segregation within the initially homogeneous phase.
Stress-induced segregation produces brittle intermetallic or ordered phases at potential crack-nucleation sites.
Relative to the homogeneous baseline, highly loaded specimens will contain precipitates at stress-concentration regions detectable by microscopy.
Relative to the baseline, highly loaded specimens will have lower fracture toughness.
Relative to the baseline, highly loaded specimens will exhibit an earlier onset of brittle fracture.
The initial homogeneous, single-phase baseline has high toughness and ductility under low or non-degrading loading conditions.
The proposed behavior is expected under high stresses and strain rates, potentially in combination with elevated or sub-zero service temperatures.
The critical stress, strain-rate threshold, and temperature window for triggering segregation and precipitation are unknown.
The hypothesis would be falsified if loaded specimens show neither detectable segregation or brittle precipitates nor a statistically significant toughness reduction relative to low-stress controls.
